extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary_biologists, and informed general readers interested in sexual selection and comparative zoology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence for attributing anatomical, behavioural, or physiological differences between the sexes to sexual rather than ordinary (natural) selection. Includes demographic, behavioural, and comparative signs that indicate mate competition or mate choice as the driving force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sexual selection from natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that give an advantage over other individuals of the same sex and species solely with respect to reproduction are due to sexual selection; characters useful for ordinary life functions arise from natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trait does not appear to increase survival or general fitness but confers advantage in acquiring mates (e.g., prehensile claspers, ornaments, weapons), infer sexual selection. Example contrasts: sensory/locomotive organs needed for ordinary life (natural selection) vs those primarily used to find or hold a mate (sexual selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-in-context test (mating vs life necessities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an organ's primary service is for mating (e.g., holding female, preventing rival access) or for other life purposes; if mainly for mating it is likely sexually selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural history observations (e.g., male moths cannot unite with females with broken tarsi; crustacean leg/antennae modified for prehension) to judge function. When function is ambiguous, note difficulty distinguishing between natural and sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-survival ornaments/weapons indicate sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures like ornaments, offensive/defensive weapons, vocal/instrumental displays, and scent glands that do not enhance survival but increase mating success are attributable to sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue sexual selection when unornamented or unarmed individuals survive and reproduce in ordinary conditions but lose mating opportunities to ornamented/armed rivals. Examples: bird plumage displays, antlers, odour glands used to allure females.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female choice (taste/discrimination) as a mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: When females exert choice among males (preferring ornamented, vigorous, or better-displaying males), sexual selection acts via female preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence that females discriminate (courtship displays, song, antics). Darwin notes that female choice implies some 'powers of discrimination and taste' and gives domestic/selective breeding analogies (game-cocks, Sebright bantam). Expect female preference to be less complex than human aesthetic taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male–male rivalry (competition) as a mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: When males fight or exert dominance to gain access to females, traits that confer advantage in these contests are sexually selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe contests and victors gaining mates (e.g., fighting males, males with better weapons). Analogy to artificial selection: victors in cockfights used to improve breeds. Consider both direct possession of females and prevention of rivals' access as selective benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal advantage (earlier maturity/arrival) promotes sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Males (or females) that arrive earlier at breeding grounds or mature earlier can secure more matings and thus drive selection for traits associated with early breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use migration and phenology data (males of migratory birds, salmon, many insects maturing before females) to infer selection favoring earlier breeders. Consider maternal/seasonal constraints limiting female shift in maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assortative pairing of vigorous individuals amplifies selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When the most vigorous, well-nourished, and early-breeding individuals pair together, their higher reproductive success concentrates advantages and can amplify sexual selection on associated male traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for pairing patterns where vigorous males pair with vigorous early-breeding females and rear more and healthier offspring (evidence from brood comparisons and timing of broods). References: Jenner Weir, J.A. Allen observations on brood quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-ratio and local numerical excess influence sexual selection strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A numerical preponderance of males (or occasional/local male excess) increases competition and makes sexual selection more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess birth and maturity sex ratios and local fluctuations. Domesticated statistics (race-horses, greyhounds) and wild estimates are informative but may differ from natural conditions. Even temporary or local male excess can leave lasting effects across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of polygamy on sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Polygamy (males securing multiple females) produces the same selective pressure as male numerical excess by leaving many males unpaired and favoring the strongest or most attractive males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine mating system (polygamous vs monogamous). Correlate presence/intensity of secondary sexual characters with polygamy (e.g., seals, many ruminants, peacock). Note exceptions and taxa where monogamous species still show strong sexual dimorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral asymmetry: males as seekers and females as choosers
rubrics_metrics.description: When males actively seek and court and females are coy/passive, selection disproportionately modifies males (behavioural roles predict sex-biased trait elaboration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use widespread natural-history observations (males more eager in birds, mammals, insects; females often require courting). Infer that active male behavior promotes development of secondary sexual characters in males.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asses variability differences between sexes
rubrics_metrics.description: If one sex (usually males) exhibits greater variability and tendency to vary, sexual selection can act more strongly on that sex and produce greater modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare variation in domestic and natural populations (Von Nathusius, domesticated breeds, human sexual dimorphism). Higher male variability can facilitate accumulation of sexually selected traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental/defensive contribution amplifies male selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If males defend or assist females (during pairing or in provisioning young), male choice or male-conferred advantages can shape sexual selection dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess natural history for male parental help or defense. In species where males defend females or help provide food for young, selection may favor males that can secure and support mates, influencing both mate choice and competition outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative distribution of dimorphism across taxa as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns across groups (which taxa show sexual differences and their mating systems) inform whether sexual selection explains observed traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey comparative data (mammals, birds, reptiles, fishes, insects). Examples: strong dimorphism in polygamous ungulates and marine seals, varied results in birds (some monogamous species highly dimorphic), and near absence in some small orders (rodents). Use concordance between mating system and dimorphism to support sexual selection hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestication experiments and artificial selection as analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Human selective breeding shows how mate preferences and selective pairing can produce rapid changes in ornamentation and carriage; these analogies support sexual selection mechanisms in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite domestic examples (game-cocks, Sebright bantam, domestic ducks becoming polygamous and showing different pairing outcomes) to illustrate how selection on mate-attraction traits operates and can change mating systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-out survival benefit (counterfactual of equal survival)
rubrics_metrics.description: When females (or the unornamented/less-armed sex) survive and reproduce as well as or better than ornamented/armed males in ordinary life, the trait is unlikely due to ordinary natural selection and more likely sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare survival/procreative success of sexes or phenotypes in non-mating contexts. If unornamented individuals are viable but lose reproductive opportunities to ornamented rivals, infer sexual selection (Darwin's argument about females being unornamented yet surviving).
